In brief

Caught in her feverish fantasy of meeting Mister Right (earlier in Nausicaa she has yearned for "a manly man with a strong quiet face who had not found his ideal"), Gerty MacDowell remembers a moving poem she read in a newspaper: "Art thou real, my ideal?" To this question one might reply: Of course not, you idiot, it's the nature of ideals to exceed reality, and reality inevitably falls short of them. The verse sounds like one that Joyce might have cooked up in a savagely playful moment, but Stephen Hero indicates that he found it in an actual poem he encountered at university. There it is attributed to a fictional character, "Hughes," but Nausicaa pegs it to a real person, one Louis J. Walsh. In giving the author his real name, Joyce finished the job of settling scores with an old adversary.

At more length

Gerty feels "that she too could write poetry if she could only express herself like that poem that appealed to her so deeply that she had copied out of the newspaper she found one evening round the potherbs. Art thou real, my ideal? it was called by Louis J. Walsh, Magherafelt, and after there was something about twilight, wilt thou ever? and ofttimes the beauty of poetry, so sad in its transient loveliness, had misted her eyes with silent tears that the years were slipping by for her, one by one." This encounter with a poem in a newspaper (one that Joyce demeans by wrapping produce in it) reprises one in Stephen Hero, when a student named Madden tells Stephen that Hughes "writes for our paper." He hands Stephen a handwritten poem, presumably submitted to him for publication. Consisting of four stanzas of eight lines each, it is titled My Ideal.

Each stanza began with the words "Art thou real?" The poem told of the poet's troubles in a "vale of woe" and of the "heart-throbs" which these troubles caused him. It told of "weary nights" and "anxious days" and of an "unquenchable desire" for an excellence beyond that "which earth can give." After this mournful idealism the final stanza offered a certain consolatory, hypothetical alternative to the poet in his woes: it began somewhat hopefully:
Art thou real, my Ideal?
Wilt thou ever come to me
In the soft and gentle twilight
With your baby on your knee?
The effect of this apparition on Stephen was a long staining blush of anger. The tawdry lines, the futile change of number ["thou," "your"], the ludicrous waddling approach of Hughes's "Ideal" weighed down by an inexplicable infant combined to cause him a sharp agony in the sensitive region. (82-83)

As a particularly execrable example of the vague, romantically dreamy verse associated with the Celtic Twilight, these lines would by themselves be sufficient to excite Joyce's wrath. But the animus was intensified by his personal dislike of the man who wrote them.

In My Brother's Keeper, Stanislaus Joyce quotes the quatrain and identifies its author, "the boy orator," as "The student from Magherafelt, to whom I have already alluded, Walsh by name" (165). Louis Joseph Walsh was actually born and raised in Maghera, another town in County Derry. Two years older than James Joyce, he was studying law at University College Dublin at the same time that Joyce was pursuing an undergraduate degree there. The two men clashed on multiple occasions, most of them associated with the Literary and Historical Society, a UCD debating union established by John Henry Newman at the university's outset in 1855. Richard Ellmann notes that in February 1899 Walsh defeated Joyce in voting for the society's treasurer (70) and in 1900 again defeated Joyce for the society's gold medal for oratory (96). In February 1902 Joyce read a paper on James Clarence Mangan to the society that was exceptionally well received by most of the audience, but Walsh rose to accuse him of "unpatriotically ignoring the fact that Mangan was one of the men of '48" (96). The notion that literature must be subordinate to politics was anathema to Joyce, gospel to Walsh.

But the antipathy ran even deeper than that. Stanislaus observes that Walsh's attack on the Mangan lecture was personal, "based not on the paper but on 'The Day of the Rabblement'. And perhaps not altogether on that either" (165). The final sentence is supported by another passage in Stephen Hero which describes "Hughes" objecting to Stephen's advocacy not of Mangan but of some "foreign" writer. The reference is most likely to a major paper on Ibsen, titled "Drama and Life," that Joyce had delivered to the society two years earlier, in 1900. Joyce presents Hughes as not only insisting that Irish literature must advance Irish nationalist ambitions but also believing that literature of a broader scope is morally dangerous and should be suppressed:

The climax of aggressiveness was reached when Hughes stood up. He declared in ringing Northern accents that the moral welfare of the Irish people was "menaced by such theories." They wanted no foreign filth. Mr Daedalus might read what authors he liked, of course, but the Irish people had their own glorious literature where they could always find fresh ideals to spur them on to new patriotic endeavours. Mr Daedalus was himself a renegade from the Nationalist ranks: he professed cosmopolitism. But a man that was of all countries was of no country—you must first have a nation before you have art. (103)

There can be little doubt that to these two passionate idealists their disagreements felt like matters of life and death. To people looking on from a distance, they may seem more like temperamental differences. On 16 June 1986, Gerry Moriarty published an article about Walsh in The Irish Press titled "James and Louis never did get on." The column was informed by conversations with Walsh's daughter Sheila, a wedding columnist in the same paper. Moriarty writes, "The two just never hit if off because they were so utterly different in character, temperament and outlook—Joyce the irreligious, revolutionary literary genius; Walsh the pious Gaelic Leaguer and dedicated Sinn Feiner happy in the conservative literary values of the period.... It was obvious that the two men had nothing in common, says Sheila. Her father was religious while Joyce was avowedly not. He was also a republican while Joyce, having flirted with the idea, was fervently indifferent to the cause." As for Joyce's mistake about where Walsh hailed from, Sheila offered an explanation: although her grandfather Louis kept a hotel in Maghera, her granduncle John had a hotel in nearby Magherafelt.

The Hughes of Stephen Hero is "a great enthusiast" for Irish nationhood, and Stephen scorns him: "One of these days he will be a barrister, a Q.C. [Queen's Counsel], perhaps a judge—and yet he sneers at the Parliamentary Party because they take an oath of allegiance" (63). After graduation Walsh practiced law as a solicitor in Maghera and continued to pursue nationalist politics. Sheila Walsh says that he "was active in the Republican struggle, topping the poll in a county council election in Co. Antrim in 1920 and twice unsuccessfully seeking election in the constituency for North Antrim during that period. He was in jail twice, escaping from Co. Derry once." After independence Walsh was made a district judge in County Donegal, the only part of Ulster that opted to leave the United Kingdom. He continued to write. Sheila Walsh says that her father, "still remembered in Donegal as a witty, compassionate justice[,] would have preferred journalism or full-time writing to law. He wrote a weekly column for The Derry Journal using the pseudonym Cormac Mac Art."  He also published five books and plays, including the comedy The Pope in Killybuck, which according to Walsh's son Louis "earned the rare distinction of provoking Orange audiences to believe it was a skit on Nationalists while Nationalists took a totally opposite interpretation." The play was revived in the 1980s, he notes, and had "a successful run in the north."

The paragraphs above have sketched a fairly broad highway of details connecting Hughes and Walsh. But two dusty side tracks can also be observed, one leading to a second real-life model and the other to a second literary character. Stephen Hero introduces Hughes as the teacher of an Irish language class that Stephen is taking:

The teacher was a young man in spectacles with a very sick-looking face and a very crooked mouth. He spoke in a high-pitched voice and with a cutting Northern accent. He never lost an opportunity of sneering at seoninism [West Britonism] and at those who would not learn their native tongue. He said that Beurla [English] was the language of commerce and Irish the speech of the soul and he had two witticisms which always made his class laugh. One was the 'Almighty Dollar' and the other was the 'Spiritual Saxon'. Everyone regarded Mr Hughes as a great enthusiast and some thought he had a great career before him as an orator. On Friday nights when there was a public meeting of the League he often spoke but as he did not know enough Irish he always excused himself at the beginning of his speech for having to speak to the audience in the language of the 'Spiritual Saxon'. At the end of every speech he quoted a piece of verse. He scoffed very much at Trinity College and at the Irish Parliamentary Party. He could not regard as patriots men who had taken oaths of allegiance to the Oueen of England and he could not regard as a national university an institution which did not express the religious convictions of the majority of the Irish people. His speeches were always loudly applauded and Stephen heard some of the audience say that they were sure he would be a great success at the bar. On enquiry, Stephen found that Hughes, who was the son of a Nationalist solicitor in Armagh, was a law-student at the King’s Inns. (59-60)

The identification of Hughes as a teacher of Irish is odd, because it is known that Joyce studied Irish, briefly, with Patrick Pearse. Most of the passage seems intended as a portrait of Walsh (boy orator, future barrister, northern Irish upbringing, ardent nationalism, religious piety, fancier of verse), but Vivien Igoe notes that Walsh, like Joyce, studied Irish with Pearse. Why does the novel show Hughes teaching Irish, a language that he does not know well enough to converse in?

To resolve the seeming contradictions one might hypothesize that Walsh, like Joyce, was learning the language from Pearse while simultaneously conducting a beginner's study group of his own. But it seems much more likely that Joyce has muddied the waters by including qualities of Pearse in the character called Hughes. Pearse liked to ridicule the inadequacies of English in his class—Joyce quit after hearing him mock the word "thunder," one of his favorites. A bit later in Stephen Hero, after reading the offensive "Art thou real, my ideal?," Stephen decides that "attendance in Mr Hughes's class was no longer possible for him" (83). The conflation of two real-life models in one character feels a bit awkward, but there is a clear logic to it. Pearse too was an ardent nationalist (one of the leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising, shot by firing squad for his pains), he too wrote poems (in both English and Irish), and having been born on 10 November 1879 he was at most one year older than Walsh. Joyce apparently saw similarities in the two men and decided to kill both birds with one stone.

When he revised his failed novel into A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, he included in part 5 many of the kinds of scenes of university life that had preoccupied him before, and it seems possible that he now redrafted the figure of Hughes. Gerry Moriarty infers that in this second go Joyce fictionalized Walsh as a student named MacAlister. MacAlister plays a smaller part in the new novel, but the strong repulsive force that separates Joyce from Walsh and Stephen from Hughes radiates off the page once more: "Stephen looked coldly on the oblong skull beneath him overgrown with tangled twinecoloured hair. The voice, the accent, the mind of the questioner offended him and he allowed the offence to carry him towards wilful unkindness, bidding his mind think that the student’s father would have done better had he sent his son to Belfast to study and have saved something on the train fare by so doing."

Louis Joseph Walsh died in 1942 and was buried in the Conwal cemetery in Letterkenny. My journey into learning more about him and obtaining a photograph started with this fact. A friend in Derry, Vincent Van Wyk, noted that the gravesite in Letterkenny seemed well tended and suggested that I write a letter to the Walsh family which could be printed off, wrapped in weatherproof plastic, and placed next to the gravestone. We undertook these steps, and some time later I received an email from one of Louis's grandsons. Brian Walsh, comically observing that he felt "like a character from a John Le Carré novel," related that the mysterious letter had reached him after passing through the hands of one cousin and five siblings. He sent me a 1986 article from a now-defunct Irish newspaper that quoted the reminiscences of his aunt and uncle and featured exactly the kind of university photograph I was hoping to find. Such is the labyrinthine adventure of tracking down Joyce's references to real people in a country where people remember people who knew those people.

John Hunt 2026
